## Do Kegels Help With Premature Ejaculation? What Research Says
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/do-kegels-help-premature-ejaculation/
Last reviewed: 2026-08-04

> **Quick answer:** Pelvic floor rehabilitation may help some men with premature ejaculation, but studies are limited and often use supervised, multimodal programs. There is no proven universal home-Kegel protocol.

> **Medical note:** Premature ejaculation is a recognized medical condition. A clinician is the correct first stop for diagnosis and personal treatment guidance.

Pelvic floor muscle rehabilitation may help some men with premature ejaculation, but the evidence is based on a limited number of relatively small studies.

The results are promising. They are not a guarantee, and they do not establish one standard home Kegel protocol.

## What Does the Research Actually Show?

One of the most cited studies was published by Pastore and colleagues in 2014.

The study included 40 men with lifelong premature ejaculation and a baseline intravaginal ejaculatory latency time of one minute or less.

Participants completed a 12-week pelvic floor rehabilitation program. The program was more involved than downloading a timer and doing unsupervised contractions.

It included professional rehabilitation components such as:

- Pelvic floor muscle training.
- Biofeedback.
- Electrical stimulation.
- Repeated supervised sessions.

The authors reported that 33 of 40 participants gained control over the ejaculatory reflex by the end of the program, with mean measured latency increasing during the study.

That result deserves attention, but it must not be used as a personal success rate. It also needs context:

- The sample was small.
- There was no large multicenter randomized trial establishing a universal effect.
- The intervention combined several rehabilitation methods.
- The participants had lifelong PE under defined study criteria.
- The result does not prove that generic home Kegels produce the same outcome.

## What Did Later Studies and Reviews Find?

A 2018 paper reported longer-term outcomes from pelvic floor rehabilitation in men with lifelong PE.

A 2019 systematic review concluded that pelvic floor muscle training appeared helpful for erectile dysfunction and premature ejaculation. It also found substantial variation in:

- Program length.
- Exercise frequency.
- Intensity.
- Therapist contact.
- Additional interventions.
- Study quality.

The authors could not identify one optimal protocol.

A [systematic review and meta-analysis published in May 2026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42132359/) adds newer evidence. Its results were not a simple endorsement: pelvic floor muscle training and sphincter-control training showed a smaller effect on measured latency than the control interventions used in the included studies. The practical conclusion remains cautious because protocols, control treatments, and study quality vary.

## Why Might the Pelvic Floor Affect Ejaculatory Control?

Ejaculation involves coordinated activity across the nervous system, reproductive tract, pelvic floor, and muscles around the urethra.

Pelvic floor muscles including the bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus participate in sexual function and the expulsion phase of ejaculation.

Training may help through:

- Better awareness of pelvic muscle activity.
- Improved voluntary control.
- Improved ability to contract at the intended time.
- Better relaxation and coordination.
- Reduced confusion between arousal, tension, and deliberate contraction.

This is a proposed mechanism, not proof that stronger contractions alone solve PE.

An overactive pelvic floor may also contribute to pain or poor coordination. Constant squeezing is not the goal.

## What Did the Research Protocols Look Like?

The best-known Pastore program lasted 12 weeks.

It was a rehabilitation program rather than a simple daily rep count. Published descriptions include physiokinesiotherapy, biofeedback, and electrical stimulation delivered across repeated sessions.

That makes the study difficult to copy at home.

Do not reduce a supervised multimodal program to:

> “Do 100 Kegels every day for 12 weeks.”

The research does not support that shortcut.

A physical therapist may use assessment, feedback, breathing, relaxation, and coordination work alongside strengthening.

## Where Does Pelvic Floor Training Sit Among Established Options?

[Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/mens-health/in-depth/kegel-exercises-for-men/art-20045074) lists several categories used in PE management:

- Behavioral techniques.
- Pelvic floor exercises.
- Counseling or sex therapy.
- Clinician-prescribed medication.
- Combinations of approaches.

The correct option depends on whether PE is lifelong or acquired, whether erectile dysfunction is also present, medication use, psychological factors, relationship context, pelvic pain, and other health conditions.

This article does not recommend one option.

The [AUA/SMSNA guideline](https://www.auanet.org/guidelines-and-quality/guidelines/disorders-of-ejaculation) discusses behavioral and clinician-directed medical approaches. A urologist or sexual medicine clinician can evaluate the wider picture.

## Why Is Seeing a Doctor Important?

Acquired PE can be associated with other problems, including erectile dysfunction, prostatitis, thyroid conditions, medication changes, anxiety, or relationship factors.

A clinician can help determine:

- Whether the symptoms fit a recognized PE pattern.
- Whether the problem is lifelong or acquired.
- Whether erectile dysfunction is contributing.
- Whether pain, urinary symptoms, or pelvic tension are present.
- Whether medication or another condition may be involved.
- Whether pelvic floor physical therapy is appropriate.

Embarrassment is common. It is not a reason to rely on anonymous promises.

## Can Doing More Kegels Make PE Worse?

Possibly, when the pelvic floor is already overactive or poorly coordinated.

Stop self-directed strengthening and seek assessment if you have:

- Pelvic pain.
- Urinary urgency.
- Difficulty starting urine.
- Pain after ejaculation.
- A constant gripping sensation.
- Symptoms that worsen after contractions.

Read [Can You Do Too Many Kegels?](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/can-you-do-too-many-kegels/) for the difference between weakness and overactivity.

## What Are Realistic Expectations?

The honest expectation is uncertainty.

Pelvic floor rehabilitation:

- May help some men.
- Usually requires weeks or months, not days.
- May involve professional supervision.
- May work better as part of a broader plan.
- Does not have one proven universal protocol.
- Is not appropriate for every pelvic floor pattern.

Do not use a single study percentage as a personal forecast.

Study participants are not interchangeable with every person reading a blog.

For general training timelines, read [How Long Does It Take for Kegels to Work for Men?](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/how-long-do-kegels-take-to-work-for-men/).

For conservative exercise volume, read [How Many Kegels Should a Man Do Per Day?](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/how-many-kegels-a-day-for-men/).

## Use Guided Timing for Quick Squeezes, Holds, and Relaxation

Home pelvic floor training usually mixes quick squeezes, longer holds, and full relaxation between them. Kegel Morse Hero turns that mix into Morse-code rhythms: short signals for quick squeezes, long signals for holds, and pauses for recovery, with haptic cues so you can train discreetly. It does not diagnose or treat premature ejaculation, measure muscle activation, or guarantee results.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How long do Kegels take to help premature ejaculation?

The best-known rehabilitation studies used programs lasting around 12 weeks. That does not guarantee improvement at 12 weeks, and the programs included professional components beyond ordinary home Kegels.

### Are reverse Kegels better for premature ejaculation?

There is no strong evidence establishing reverse Kegels as a universal answer. Relaxation may matter when the pelvic floor is overactive, but forceful bearing down is not appropriate self-treatment.

### Can I manage premature ejaculation without a doctor?

A clinician can identify contributing conditions and explain established options. Self-directed exercises may miss erectile dysfunction, pelvic pain, medication effects, or other causes.

### Are Kegels a first-line option for PE?

Pelvic floor exercises are included among possible management approaches by major clinical sources, but personal recommendations depend on the individual. The evidence base is smaller than online marketing often suggests.

*This article is for general education and is not medical advice. See a pelvic floor physical therapist, urologist, or sexual medicine clinician for personal guidance.*

## Kegel Exercises for Women: A Safe, Effective Beginner's Guide
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/kegel-exercises-for-women/
Last reviewed: 2026-09-22

The pelvic floor is a group of muscles and connective tissues that supports the bladder, uterus, rectum, and other structures inside the pelvis. These muscles also help control urination and bowel movements and contribute to sexual function.

Like any muscle group, the pelvic floor can lose strength or coordination. Pregnancy, childbirth, aging, surgery, chronic coughing, constipation, and other factors may contribute. Kegel exercises—also called pelvic floor muscle training—can help when weakness is part of the problem.

However, Kegels are not simply about squeezing as hard as possible. Correct technique includes both contraction and complete relaxation.

## Potential Benefits of Kegel Exercises

Regular pelvic floor training may help:

- Reduce urine leakage during coughing, laughing, running, or jumping
- Improve bowel control
- Support recovery after pregnancy and childbirth
- Improve awareness and coordination of the pelvic floor
- Support sexual function for some women

Results vary, and not every pelvic floor problem is caused by weakness. Pain, difficulty emptying the bladder, or discomfort during sex can sometimes involve muscles that are already too tense.

## How to Find the Correct Muscles

Imagine that you are trying to prevent yourself from passing gas while also stopping urine. You should feel a gentle closing and lifting sensation inside the pelvis.

You can interrupt urine flow once to help identify the muscles, but do not make this your regular exercise. Repeatedly stopping urine can interfere with normal bladder emptying.

During a correct Kegel:

- The sensation should be a squeeze and lift, not a downward push
- Your breathing should remain natural
- Your thighs, buttocks, and abdominal muscles should stay mostly relaxed
- The pelvic floor should release fully afterward

If you cannot locate the muscles, a pelvic floor physiotherapist can assess your technique.

## Basic Slow Kegels

Slow contractions build endurance.

1. Lie down or sit in a comfortable position.
2. Gently tighten and lift the pelvic floor.
3. Hold for three seconds.
4. Relax completely for three to five seconds.
5. Repeat five times.

As control improves, gradually work toward 8–10 repetitions and holds of up to five seconds. Avoid straining to reach a particular number.

## Quick Contractions

Fast contractions train the muscles to respond to sudden pressure.

1. Squeeze the pelvic floor quickly.
2. Release immediately and completely.
3. Repeat 5–10 times.
4. Rest before performing another set.

This type of contraction may be helpful just before a cough, sneeze, or lift.

## The Pelvic Floor Elevator

This exercise develops control at different levels of effort.

1. Begin with a light contraction.
2. Increase to medium intensity.
3. Hold briefly without holding your breath.
4. Slowly reduce the contraction.
5. Relax fully at the bottom.

The goal is smooth control, not maximum force. Repeat 5–8 times.

## Bridge With Gentle Pelvic Floor Engagement

Try this only after you can isolate the pelvic floor without squeezing your buttocks excessively.

1. Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet flat.
2. Inhale and relax.
3. Exhale, gently engage the pelvic floor, and lift your hips.
4. Pause for two or three seconds while breathing normally.
5. Lower your hips and release the pelvic floor.
6. Repeat 8–10 times.

Stop if the movement creates pelvic pressure, pain, or urine leakage.

## How Often Should You Do Kegels?

A reasonable beginner routine is one set of slow contractions and one set of quick contractions once or twice daily. Increase gradually if the muscles recover comfortably.

Pelvic floor training usually requires weeks of consistent practice. Improvement may take several months, especially when treating urinary symptoms. Once your symptoms improve, a smaller maintenance routine can help preserve progress.

## Common Mistakes

Holding your breath increases abdominal pressure. Exhale gently during the contraction and continue breathing normally.

Contracting everything at once—tightening the stomach, thighs, and buttocks—can hide poor pelvic floor control. Reduce the effort and focus on the internal lift.

Skipping relaxation is a mistake too: the release phase is as important as the squeeze. A muscle that never relaxes can become painful or poorly coordinated.

Doing too many repetitions causes fatigue, which can reduce technique and contribute to discomfort. More is not automatically better.

Practising while urinating should be avoided. Use urine interruption only as a one-time identification test—not as a workout.

## When Kegels May Not Be the Right Exercise

Do not assume that every symptom requires strengthening. An overactive or tight pelvic floor may cause pelvic pain, painful sex, constipation, urinary urgency, or difficulty emptying the bladder.

Seek advice from a doctor or pelvic floor physiotherapist if:

- Kegels cause pain, pressure, or cramping
- You cannot relax after a contraction
- Urinary or bowel symptoms become worse
- You have pain during sex
- You are recovering from pelvic surgery or a complicated delivery
- Consistent practice does not improve your symptoms

The best pelvic floor program may include strengthening, relaxation, breathing, coordination work, or a combination of these approaches.

## Final Thoughts

Kegel exercises can be valuable, but technique matters more than intensity. Start gently, breathe normally, and allow a full release after every contraction. A balanced pelvic floor should be able to tighten when needed and relax when the task is over.

This article is educational and is not a diagnosis or individualized treatment plan.

## Sources

- [NIDDK: Kegel Exercises](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/kegel-exercises)
- [Mayo Clinic: Kegel Exercises for Women](https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/womens-health/in-depth/kegel-exercises/art-20045283)
- [ACOG: Your Sexual Health](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/your-sexual-health)

## Core Workouts for Women: Seven Exercises for Strength and Stability
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/core-workouts-for-women/
Last reviewed: 2026-09-22

A strong core is useful for far more than visible abdominal definition. The core helps stabilize the spine and pelvis while you walk, lift, run, exercise, and perform everyday tasks.

It includes the abdominal wall, back muscles, diaphragm, hip muscles, and pelvic floor. These structures need to coordinate rather than remain tightly braced all day.

The following exercises can be performed at home with minimal equipment. Move slowly, breathe normally, and choose the easier variation whenever you lose control.

## 1. Forearm Plank

The plank trains the abdominal wall, shoulders, back, and glutes to resist unwanted movement.

Place your forearms on the floor with elbows under the shoulders. Extend your legs and support yourself on your toes. Keep a straight line from your head to your heels. Exhale gently and tighten your abdomen without holding your breath. Hold for 10–30 seconds.

Complete 2–3 controlled sets. Beginners can keep their knees on the floor. Avoid dropping the hips, lifting them excessively, or forcing a long hold after your form breaks down.

## 2. Dead Bug

The dead bug develops trunk control while the arms and legs move independently.

Lie on your back with your arms above your chest. Lift your legs so the hips and knees are bent to approximately 90 degrees. Keep your lower back comfortably supported. Slowly lower one arm and the opposite leg. Return to the start and switch sides.

Perform 6–10 repetitions per side. Avoid moving quickly or allowing the lower back to arch sharply.

## 3. Bird Dog

The bird dog challenges balance and strengthens the back, abdominals, shoulders, and glutes.

Begin on your hands and knees. Place your hands beneath your shoulders and knees beneath your hips. Extend one arm forward and the opposite leg backward. Keep the hips and shoulders level. Pause, return slowly, and change sides.

Perform 8–10 repetitions per side. Avoid twisting the pelvis or lifting the leg higher than you can control.

## 4. Glute Bridge

The bridge trains the glutes and hamstrings while the trunk stabilizes the pelvis.

Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet flat. Exhale and press through your heels. Lift your hips until your body forms a comfortable line from shoulders to knees. Pause for two seconds, then lower slowly.

Perform 10–15 repetitions. Avoid overarching the lower back or pushing through the toes.

## 5. Modified Side Plank

The side plank targets the obliques and lateral hip muscles.

Lie on your side with your elbow under your shoulder. Bend your knees for the beginner variation. Lift your hips while keeping the head, ribs, and pelvis aligned. Hold for 10–20 seconds, then repeat on the other side.

As you become stronger, straighten the legs.

## 6. Heel Slides

Heel slides are a gentle option for learning abdominal control.

Lie on your back with both knees bent. Exhale and gently engage the lower abdomen. Slide one heel away without allowing the pelvis to rotate. Bring the heel back and switch sides.

Perform 8–12 repetitions per side.

## 7. Pelvic Floor Contractions

The pelvic floor is part of the core, but it should not remain contracted during every exercise.

Imagine stopping urine and gas at the same time. Feel a gentle squeeze and lift. Hold for three seconds while breathing normally. Relax fully for at least three seconds. Repeat 5–8 times.

Do not routinely practise while urinating. If contractions cause pelvic pain or make it difficult to relax, stop and consult a pelvic floor physiotherapist.

## A Simple 15-Minute Routine

Complete two rounds:

- Forearm plank: 20 seconds
- Dead bug: 8 repetitions per side
- Bird dog: 8 repetitions per side
- Glute bridge: 12 repetitions
- Modified side plank: 15 seconds per side
- Heel slides: 10 repetitions per side
- Pelvic floor contractions: 5 slow repetitions

Rest for 30–60 seconds between exercises when needed.

## Form and Safety Tips

- Exhale during the most difficult part of each movement
- Stop a set when you can no longer maintain control
- Progress duration or repetitions gradually
- Choose pain-free ranges of motion
- Do not constantly pull the stomach inward or clench the pelvic floor

Seek professional advice if exercise causes pelvic heaviness, urinary leakage that is worsening, abdominal bulging after pregnancy, or persistent back or pelvic pain.

## Final Thoughts

Effective core training is not about punishing abdominal workouts. It is about building coordination between the trunk, hips, breathing muscles, and pelvic floor. Consistent, well-controlled sessions can create a stronger foundation for sport and everyday movement.

People who are pregnant, newly postpartum, recovering from surgery, or managing pelvic floor symptoms may need individualized exercise guidance.

## Sources

- [FDA: What Women Need to Know About Their Pelvic Floor](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/knowledge-and-news-women-owh-blog/what-women-need-know-about-their-pelvic-floor)
- [NIDDK: Kegel Exercises](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/kegel-exercises)
- [Mayo Clinic: Kegel Exercises for Women](https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/womens-health/in-depth/kegel-exercises/art-20045283)

## Reduced Penile Sensitivity: Causes and Eight Practical Steps
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/increase-male-sensitivity/
Last reviewed: 2026-09-22

Changes in penile sensitivity can affect pleasure, orgasm, confidence, and relationships. Sometimes the change is temporary and linked to stress, fatigue, friction, or a new sexual routine. In other cases, reduced sensation may be associated with medication, diabetes, nerve problems, circulation, hormonal changes, surgery, or pelvic injury.

There is no universal trick that restores sensitivity overnight. The best approach is to reduce avoidable irritation, support general health, and investigate persistent or sudden numbness.

## What Does "Reduced Sensitivity" Mean?

People use the phrase to describe different experiences:

- Touch feels duller than before
- More pressure or stimulation is required
- Orgasm takes much longer or does not occur
- Erections are less reliable
- Part of the penis or surrounding area feels numb or tingly

These symptoms do not all have the same cause. Erectile function, arousal, sensation, ejaculation, and orgasm overlap, but they are not identical.

## Change Excessive Pressure or Friction

A very tight grip, repetitive high-pressure stimulation, long sessions, or insufficient lubrication can temporarily reduce sensation or irritate the skin.

Try lighter pressure, more variation, shorter sessions, and a suitable lubricant. Give irritated skin time to recover. Persistent numbness should not be dismissed as a habit issue without medical evaluation.

## Protect the Perineum

Long cycling sessions, an unsuitable bicycle saddle, or trauma to the area between the genitals and anus can compress nerves and blood vessels.

Check saddle fit, change position regularly, use appropriate padding, and take breaks. Stop the activity and seek medical advice if you develop lasting numbness, urinary changes, or pain.

## Support Cardiovascular and Metabolic Health

Erections and genital response depend partly on healthy blood vessels and nerves. Regular movement, blood-pressure control, and management of blood sugar can support sexual health.

Aim for a realistic combination of aerobic exercise and resistance training. If reduced sensitivity occurs alongside erectile changes, do not assume it is only a sexual issue; it may be worth discussing cardiovascular and metabolic risk with a clinician.

## Train the Pelvic Floor Carefully

Pelvic floor muscles contribute to urinary control, erection, and ejaculation. When weakness or poor coordination is present, appropriately performed pelvic floor exercises may help.

To identify the muscles, imagine stopping urine and gas at the same time. Gently squeeze and lift for three seconds, then relax for five seconds. Start with five repetitions.

Do not perform long, forceful sets or keep the muscles clenched throughout sexual activity. A tight or overactive pelvic floor can be associated with pelvic pain and ejaculation-related discomfort. Some people need relaxation and physiotherapy rather than more strengthening. For a conservative starting structure, read [How Many Kegels Should a Man Do Per Day?](/articles/how-many-kegels-a-day-for-men/)

## Review Sleep and Stress

Poor sleep, anxiety, depression, and performance pressure can reduce arousal and make physical sensation harder to notice. They can also affect erections and orgasm.

Improving sleep consistency, reducing pressure to perform, and slowing down sexual activity may help. If anxiety or low mood is persistent, professional support can be more effective than repeatedly changing techniques.

## Limit Smoking and Excessive Alcohol

Smoking damages blood vessels. Heavy alcohol use can reduce sensation, interfere with erections, and delay orgasm.

Reducing or stopping tobacco and moderating alcohol benefits overall health as well as sexual function. If cutting down is difficult, ask a healthcare professional about structured support.

## Check Medications and Health Conditions

Some antidepressants and other medications can affect libido, sensation, erection, ejaculation, or orgasm. Diabetes, neurological conditions, spinal problems, pelvic surgery, and hormonal disorders can also play a role.

Do not stop prescribed medication on your own. Ask the prescribing clinician whether your symptoms could be related and whether safe alternatives exist.

## Choose Lubricants Safely

Lubricant reduces friction and may make touch more comfortable, but it does not repair nerve damage or permanently increase sensitivity.

Use a product intended for sexual activity. Oil-based products can weaken latex condoms, while fragranced products and household oils may irritate sensitive skin. Stop using any product that causes burning, itching, or redness.

## Be Cautious With Supplements

Products marketed for testosterone, blood flow, or "male sensitivity" often make claims that are much stronger than the evidence. Supplements can interact with medications, contain inconsistent ingredients, or delay proper diagnosis.

Speak with a clinician before taking herbal products, especially if you use blood thinners, heart medication, diabetes medication, or treatment for erectile dysfunction.

## When to See a Doctor

Arrange an evaluation if sensitivity loss:

- Appears suddenly
- Persists or progressively worsens
- Follows an injury or surgery
- Occurs with weakness, back pain, or numbness elsewhere
- Is accompanied by erectile problems, urinary symptoms, sores, discharge, or testicular pain
- Causes significant distress

Sudden genital numbness combined with new leg weakness or loss of bladder or bowel control requires urgent medical attention.

## Final Thoughts

Reduced sensitivity is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Gentle changes in pressure, lubrication, sleep, exercise, and pelvic floor coordination may help, but ongoing numbness deserves a proper medical assessment. Treat the underlying cause rather than relying on oils, supplements, or aggressive exercises.

This article is educational and does not replace an examination by a qualified clinician.

## Sources

- [Mayo Clinic: Penis Health](https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/mens-health/in-depth/penis-health/art-20046175)
- [NIDDK: Perineal Injury in Males](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/perineal-injury-males)
- [Cleveland Clinic: Kegel Exercises for Men](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/22211-kegel-exercises-for-men)

## "Sperm Cramps": What Pain After Ejaculation May Actually Mean
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/pain-after-ejaculation-sperm-cramps/
Last reviewed: 2026-09-22

"Sperm cramps" is an informal internet term, not a recognized medical diagnosis. People usually use it to describe aching, pressure, cramping, or sharp pain during or after ejaculation.

The discomfort may be felt in the penis, testicles, perineum, pelvis, groin, or lower abdomen. Sperm itself does not cramp. The symptom can involve the prostate, urinary or reproductive tract, pelvic floor muscles, nerves, or other nearby structures.

Occasional mild discomfort may settle on its own, but repeated or severe pain should be evaluated rather than treated with random exercises.

## Common Symptoms

People may describe:

- Burning or sharp pain during ejaculation
- A deep ache in the pelvis or perineum
- Testicular or groin discomfort
- Cramping after orgasm
- Pain when urinating
- Urinary urgency or difficulty emptying the bladder

The pattern, duration, and associated symptoms help a clinician narrow down the cause.

## Prostatitis or Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome

Inflammation or pain associated with the prostate can cause discomfort in the perineum, penis, testicles, lower abdomen, or lower back. Some people also experience urinary symptoms or pain during or after ejaculation.

Not every case is caused by a bacterial infection. Chronic pelvic pain syndrome can involve muscle tension, nerve sensitivity, stress, and other factors.

## Pelvic Floor Overactivity

The pelvic floor contracts during ejaculation and then needs to relax. Research has found that some men with chronic pelvic pain—particularly those with ejaculation-related pain—have difficulty returning these muscles to a relaxed state.

In this situation, repeatedly performing strong Kegels may increase tension. Treatment may focus on breathing, relaxation, manual therapy, coordination, and other techniques prescribed by a pelvic floor physiotherapist. See [Can You Do Too Many Kegels?](/articles/can-you-do-too-many-kegels/) for more on overactive pelvic floors.

## Epididymitis or Other Infection

Inflammation of the epididymis can cause testicular pain, tenderness, and swelling. Urinary tract infections and sexually transmitted infections can also contribute to genital or pelvic pain.

These conditions require medical evaluation and may need prescription treatment. Exercises cannot eliminate an infection.

## Prostate or Pelvic Procedures

Surgery, radiation, or other treatment involving the prostate or pelvis may change sensation, ejaculation, or muscle function. Tell your treating clinician about new pain rather than trying to rehabilitate the area without guidance.

## Hernia, Stones, or Other Conditions

Groin hernias, urinary stones, nerve problems, and other conditions may produce pain that becomes noticeable during sexual activity. A physical examination may be necessary to distinguish them.

## Should You Do Kegels?

Kegels can help when weakness or poor activation is the problem. They are not an automatic treatment for pelvic pain.

If your pelvic floor is already tight, more contractions may increase pain or make relaxation more difficult. Do not begin an intensive strengthening program until a professional has assessed whether you need strengthening, relaxation, or both.

## What You Can Do While Arranging Care

For mild symptoms without warning signs:

- Pause activities that clearly trigger pain
- Avoid prolonged clenching of the pelvic floor
- Use slow diaphragmatic breathing and allow the lower abdomen to soften
- Apply comfortable warmth to the pelvic area
- Record when the pain occurs and any urinary or sexual symptoms

Over-the-counter pain medication may not be appropriate for everyone. Follow the label and ask a pharmacist or clinician if you take other medication, have kidney disease, ulcers, bleeding risk, or another relevant condition.

Do not self-treat with leftover antibiotics.

## When to Contact a Doctor

Arrange a medical assessment if pain is recurring, persistent, worsening, or affecting sexual activity. A primary-care clinician or urologist may ask about urinary symptoms, sexual history, medication, recent procedures, and possible infection.

Seek urgent care for:

- Sudden severe testicular pain
- Significant swelling or redness
- Fever, chills, or vomiting
- Blood in urine or semen
- Inability to urinate
- Pain following a significant injury

## Final Thoughts

Pain after ejaculation is real, but "sperm cramps" is too vague to explain its cause. Prostatitis, infection, pelvic floor overactivity, and other conditions can produce similar symptoms.

The most important point is that pain does not always mean the pelvic floor is weak. Stronger Kegels may be the wrong solution when the muscles cannot relax. Persistent symptoms deserve proper evaluation and an individualized plan.

This article provides general information and cannot diagnose the cause of pelvic or testicular pain.

- [PubMed: Pelvic Floor Relaxation in Men With Ejaculation-Related Pain](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35576002/)
- [PubMed: Pelvic Floor Trigger Points and Chronic Pelvic Pain](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19837420/)

## Is Edging Bad for Testosterone? What the Evidence Actually Says
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/edging-and-testosterone/
Last reviewed: 2026-09-22

Edging means approaching orgasm and then reducing or stopping stimulation so that climax is delayed. A person may repeat this cycle during masturbation or partnered sex.

Online claims describe edging as either a powerful testosterone booster or a cause of hormonal "exhaustion." Current evidence does not support either extreme.

There is no good evidence that occasional edging causes a meaningful, lasting reduction in testosterone. There is also no convincing evidence that it creates a useful long-term testosterone increase.

## What Happens During Edging?

Sexual arousal involves changes in blood flow, nervous-system activity, muscle tension, attention, and hormones. These responses naturally fluctuate throughout sexual activity.

Short-term hormonal changes during arousal or abstinence should not be confused with a lasting improvement or decline in baseline testosterone. A diagnosis of low testosterone requires appropriate symptoms and properly timed blood testing—not an assumption based on sexual habits.

## Possible Benefits

Some people use edging to:

- Learn how arousal builds
- Practise delaying orgasm
- Extend a sexual experience
- Communicate preferences with a partner
- Explore different rhythms and levels of stimulation

These are subjective or skill-based benefits. They are not proof of hormonal enhancement.

## Temporary Aching or Pressure

Prolonged arousal without orgasm may cause temporary genital heaviness or discomfort. This sensation is generally not dangerous and usually fades with time, reduced stimulation, or orgasm.

No one is obligated to provide sexual activity to relieve another person's discomfort.

## Skin Irritation or Numbness

Long sessions, high friction, strong vibration, or excessive pressure may irritate the skin or temporarily dull sensation. Use lubricant, change technique, and stop when discomfort begins.

Persistent numbness, bruising, or pain requires medical advice.

## Pelvic Floor Tension

Arousal and orgasm involve the pelvic floor. Repeatedly clenching these muscles for a long time may contribute to fatigue or tension in susceptible people.

After a contraction, allow the pelvic floor to release fully. If edging causes pelvic pain, painful ejaculation, urinary urgency, or difficulty relaxing, take a break and consider evaluation by a pelvic floor physiotherapist. See [Can You Do Too Many Kegels?](/articles/can-you-do-too-many-kegels/) for more on overactive pelvic floor symptoms.

## Performance Pressure

Edging can become counterproductive if the person becomes preoccupied with timing, duration, or avoiding orgasm. Sexual activity should not feel like a test of discipline.

If the practice causes anxiety, conflict, loss of sleep, soreness, or compulsive behaviour, reduce or stop it.

## Does Ejaculation Lower Testosterone?

Research on ejaculation, abstinence, and testosterone is limited and often based on small studies. Temporary fluctuations have been reported, but they do not demonstrate that normal ejaculation lowers testosterone in a clinically meaningful way.

Testosterone is influenced by many factors, including age, sleep, body composition, illness, medication, and testicular or pituitary function. Sexual frequency alone is not a reliable way to diagnose or manage low testosterone.

## How to Practise Edging More Comfortably

- Use sufficient lubricant
- Reduce pressure and speed before discomfort appears
- Keep sessions within a comfortable duration
- Breathe normally instead of bracing the abdomen
- Avoid continuous maximum-effort Kegels
- Let the pelvic floor soften during pauses
- Communicate clearly with a partner and respect consent
- Stop if you experience pain, numbness, or distress

There is no medically required number of cycles and no health benefit to pushing through discomfort.

## How to Support Healthy Testosterone

If your goal is general hormonal health, focus on factors with clearer evidence:

- Get adequate, consistent sleep
- Perform regular resistance and aerobic exercise
- Maintain a sustainable body weight
- Eat enough overall energy, protein, and dietary fat
- Limit excessive alcohol
- Treat sleep apnea and other medical conditions
- Discuss symptoms and testing with a healthcare professional

Do not take testosterone or "testosterone boosters" without appropriate evaluation. Testosterone therapy has real indications, risks, and monitoring requirements.

## When to Seek Medical Advice

Contact a clinician if you have persistent low libido, erectile difficulties, loss of morning erections, infertility concerns, testicular changes, unexplained fatigue, or other symptoms associated with low testosterone.

Seek advice sooner if sexual activity causes recurrent pelvic pain, painful ejaculation, blood in urine or semen, or persistent numbness.

## Final Thoughts

Edging is neither a proven testosterone hack nor a known cause of hormonal collapse. For most people, occasional edging is a matter of preference. The main concerns are comfort, irritation, pelvic floor tension, consent, and whether the practice begins to cause distress.

Use it as an optional sexual technique—not as a hormone treatment. Only a qualified clinician can diagnose testosterone deficiency or the cause of persistent sexual symptoms.

## Sources

- [Mayo Clinic: Male Hypogonadism](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/male-hypogonadism/symptoms-causes/syc-20354881)
- [Cleveland Clinic: Temporary Discomfort From Arousal Without Orgasm](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/blue-balls)
- [PubMed: Ejaculation and Serum Testosterone](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12659241/)

## Am I Doing Kegels Wrong? 7 Signs and Fixes
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/am-i-doing-kegels-wrong/
Last reviewed: 2026-09-22

Kegels look simple: squeeze, hold, release. But a lot of people do them in a way that does nothing—or even makes things worse. If you're wondering "am I doing Kegels wrong?", check these seven signs.

## You Hold Your Breath

Sign: you realize at the end of a set that you haven't breathed. Fix: breathe normally the whole time. Try exhaling gently as you squeeze and inhaling as you release.

## Your Butt, Thighs or Abs Tighten

Sign: you can see or feel your glutes clench or your belly pull in. Fix: put a hand on your stomach and one on your butt. Both should stay soft. Only the pelvic floor moves—an upward, inward lift.

## You Get a Headache, Back Pain or Stomach Ache

Sign: discomfort anywhere after a session. Fix: Kegels shouldn't hurt. Pain usually means breath-holding or recruiting the wrong muscles. Go back to lying down, lower the intensity, and re-find the right muscles.

## You Never Fully Relax

Sign: you rush from one squeeze to the next. Fix: the release matters as much as the squeeze. Relax for at least as long as you held—longer if needed. A muscle that can't relax isn't a healthy muscle.

## You Do Them While Peeing

Sign: you use the toilet as your regular Kegel time. Fix: stopping your stream is only for identifying the muscles, at most once a month. Regular practice while urinating can disrupt normal bladder emptying.

## You Overdo It

Sign: hundreds of reps a day, sore or tense feeling in the pelvis. Fix: more isn't better. A few sets of about 10 reps a day is plenty. Overtraining can leave the pelvic floor tight and tense instead of strong. See [Can You Do Too Many Kegels?](/articles/can-you-do-too-many-kegels/) for more on this.

## You Expect Results in a Week

Sign: you quit after 10 days because "nothing changed." Fix: most people notice changes after 6–8 weeks of regular practice. The first month is about learning control; visible results come later.

## Bonus: You Only Ever Squeeze

Some people—especially men with a tense pelvic floor—also need reverse Kegels: deliberately relaxing and lengthening the same muscles. If you feel tight, have pelvic pain, or Kegels make symptoms worse, a pelvic floor physical therapist can tell you which one you need.

## A Correct Kegel in One Line

Lift inward like you're holding in gas, breathe, hold 3 seconds, release fully 3 seconds—nothing else moves.

Kegel Morse Hero guides every session with short squeezes and long holds (Morse code dots and dashes) and built-in rest, so you don't rush, over-train, or lose count.

## How to Find Your Pelvic Floor Muscles (Men)
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/how-to-find-pelvic-floor-muscles-men/
Last reviewed: 2026-09-22

Before Kegels can do anything for you, you need to squeeze the right muscles. That sounds obvious, but it's where most men go wrong. Mayo Clinic Health System estimates that about 40% of people don't do a Kegel correctly on the first try.

Here's how to find your pelvic floor muscles as a man, in a few minutes.

## What the Pelvic Floor Actually Is

The pelvic floor is a group of muscles stretching from your pubic bone to your tailbone, like a hammock under your pelvis. It supports the bladder and bowel, and it plays a role in erections and ejaculation.

You can't see it, which is why it's tricky to train.

## Method 1: The "Hold in Gas" Test

Imagine you're in a quiet room and need to stop yourself from passing gas. The muscles you tighten to do that are your pelvic floor.

This is the easiest and most reliable cue for most men.

## Method 2: The Mid-Stream Test (Once Only)

While urinating, try to slow or stop the stream. The muscles that do this are part of the pelvic floor.

Use this only to identify the muscles, and not more than about once a month. Doing Kegels while peeing regularly can interfere with normal bladder emptying.

## Method 3: The Perineum Check

Lie on your back and place a finger on the perineum—the area between the scrotum and anus. Squeeze as if holding in gas. You should feel the area lift slightly upward and inward.

Another visual cue: standing in front of a mirror, a correct squeeze makes the base of the penis pull in slightly and the testicles lift.

## Mistakes That Mean You're Squeezing the Wrong Muscles

- Clenching your butt. If your glutes tighten, you're compensating.
- Tightening your thighs. Legs stay relaxed.
- Sucking in your belly. Abs stay soft.
- Holding your breath. Breathe normally throughout.
- Pushing down instead of lifting up. A Kegel is an upward, inward lift.

If you feel pain in your stomach, back or head afterward, that's usually a sign you're recruiting the wrong muscles or holding your breath.

## Your First Kegel, Step by Step

1. Lie on your back, knees bent, fully relaxed.
2. Squeeze the "hold in gas" muscles and lift inward.
3. Hold for 3 seconds.
4. Release completely for 3 seconds.
5. Repeat 10 times.

Once this feels easy lying down, try it sitting, then standing.

## When to See a Professional

If you can't feel the muscles after a couple of weeks, or if Kegels cause pain, a pelvic floor physical therapist can help—often using biofeedback to show you exactly what you're contracting.

## Practice With Kegel Morse Hero

Once you've found the right muscles, Kegel Morse Hero gives you short, guided daily sessions: quick squeezes and long holds become Morse code dots and dashes, so training feels like a game instead of counting.

## Kegel Exercise Games: Making Pelvic Floor Training Less Boring
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/kegel-exercise-game/
Last reviewed: 2026-09-22

Ask anyone who has tried Kegels why they stopped. The answer is almost never "they didn't work." It's "I got bored" or "I forgot." A Kegel exercise game fixes exactly that problem.

## The Real Reason Kegel Routines Fail

Classic Kegel instructions go like this: squeeze for 3 seconds, relax for 3 seconds, repeat 10 times, three times a day. Every day. For weeks.

There's no feedback, no progress you can see, and no reason to look forward to it. Results take 6–8 weeks to appear, and most people quit long before that.

## What Gamification Changes

Games are built around the exact things a Kegel routine lacks:

- Clear goals. Finish this level, spell this word, beat yesterday's score.
- Instant feedback. You know right away whether you did it right.
- Visible progress. Levels, streaks and stats show you're improving even before your body does.
- Variety. Different patterns every session instead of the same count.

The result: sessions feel like a quick game instead of homework, and you actually come back tomorrow.

## How a Morse Code Kegel Game Works

Morse code is a natural fit for pelvic floor training because it's made of two signals:

- Dot: a short, quick squeeze (fast-twitch control)
- Dash: a longer hold (endurance)

Spelling a word means alternating quick contractions with sustained holds and releasing fully between them. That's close to what a well-rounded Kegel routine looks like anyway—just with a target you care about hitting.

For example, the word SOS is `... --- ...`: three quick squeezes, three long holds, three quick squeezes. That's a full mini-set without counting anything. Read [Morse Code Kegel Training](/articles/morse-code-kegel-training/) for a deeper look at how the mapping works.

## Tips for Training With a Kegel Game

- Relax completely between signals. The release matters as much as the squeeze.
- Breathe normally. Holding your breath is one of the most common Kegel mistakes.
- Squeeze only the pelvic floor. Glutes, thighs and abs stay relaxed.
- Play daily, not heavily. A short session every day beats a long one twice a week.

## Is a Kegel Game as Effective as Regular Kegels?

The muscle work is the same—contract, hold, release. What changes is how likely you are to keep doing it. Since consistency is what produces results, the version you'll actually stick with is the one that works.

## Try Kegel Morse Hero

Kegel Morse Hero is a pelvic floor trainer built around Morse code: dots and dashes become squeezes and holds, words become workouts, and streaks keep you consistent.

## Reverse Kegels for Men: The Skill You Miss When You Only Squeeze
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/reverse-kegels-for-men/
Last reviewed: 2026-09-28

You know how to squeeze. But can you actually let go afterward? If every pelvic floor session is about holding harder, the release can become an afterthought.

Reverse Kegels are a common name for deliberately relaxing and lengthening the pelvic floor. They are not a competition to push downward. For some men, learning that distinction is more useful than adding another set.

## What a Reverse Kegel Actually Means

A regular Kegel involves a lift and squeeze. Relaxation lets the muscles return from that contraction. The aim is comfortable movement, not a dramatic sensation or visible motion.

Your breathing provides a useful cue: during an easy inhale, the diaphragm descends and the pelvic floor normally lengthens. Think of allowing that movement rather than forcing it. [Plymouth's NHS relaxation guide](https://www.plymouthhospitals.nhs.uk/display-pil/pil-pelvic-floor-relaxation-5338) describes this connection.

## Tight Does Not Automatically Mean Strong

A pelvic floor that stays contracted may struggle to coordinate everyday functions. Pelvic discomfort, difficulty starting urine, constipation, or pain with ejaculation can occur with an overactive pelvic floor. They can also have other causes.

That list is a reason to get assessed, not a home diagnostic test. [Cleveland Clinic](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/22870-hypertonic-pelvic-floor) describes physical therapy as a central part of treatment for diagnosed hypertonicity.

## Try a Gentle Release

1. Lie comfortably with knees bent and your head supported.
2. Let your jaw, belly, and buttocks soften.
3. Inhale slowly through your nose, allowing your abdomen and lower ribs to expand.
4. Imagine the area underneath your pelvis becoming softer and less gripped.
5. Exhale easily. Let the breath return without adding a deliberate squeeze.

Try a few comfortable breaths. Do not hold your breath, bear down, or strain as though pushing out stool. Stop if this produces pain or worsens symptoms.

## When More Squeezing Is the Wrong Next Step

If exercise brings on pain or leaves you feeling persistently clenched, pause the provoking routine and ask a pelvic health physiotherapist for help. They can assess both contraction and release.

The [2025 AUA guideline recap](https://auanews.net/issues/articles/2025/july/august-2025/aua2025-plenary-recap-male-chronic-pelvic-pain-highlights-from-the-new-aua-guideline) discusses specialist physiotherapy for men with pelvic muscle pain, including approaches that reduce resting muscle tension. This is tailored care for assessed patients, not evidence that every man needs reverse Kegels.

## Should You Stop Regular Kegels?

That depends on why you are training. Some people need strengthening; others need relaxation or a combination. A clinician can help decide when symptoms are present.

For a technique refresher, see [How to Find Your Pelvic Floor Muscles](/articles/how-to-find-pelvic-floor-muscles-men/). If your main concern is piling on repetitions, read [Can You Do Too Many Kegels?](/articles/can-you-do-too-many-kegels/).

## Where Guided Training Fits

Kegel Morse Hero provides timing cues for squeeze-and-rest sessions. Use it when strengthening suits your plan; it cannot assess resting muscle tension or replace treatment for pelvic pain.

## Dribbling After Peeing? Why That Last Drop Happens
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/dribbling-after-peeing-men/
Last reviewed: 2026-09-28

You finish, wait, get dressed—and then a few drops escape. It is frustrating precisely because you thought you were done.

This is often called post-micturition dribble, or after-dribble. It can happen at different ages. The useful question is whether those drops are left in the outlet tube or whether you are having a broader problem emptying your bladder.

## Why the Last Drop Waits Until You Move

A small amount of urine can remain in the urethra, the tube carrying urine out of the body. Movement then lets it escape. Pelvic floor muscles help clear that tube, which explains why they can be part of the solution.

The [Gloucestershire Hospitals NHS guide](https://www.gloshospitals.nhs.uk/your-visit/patient-information-leaflets/after-dribble-post-micturition-dribble/) explains this mechanism and a gentle clearing technique.

## A Technique to Ask About

After urinating normally, wait a few seconds. With clean hands, place fingertips on the perineum, roughly three finger-widths behind the scrotum. Apply gentle pressure and move forward beneath the scrotum toward the base of the penis. Then clear the remaining drops normally.

This is sometimes called urethral milking. It should not hurt or involve force. If you have recently had surgery, ask your care team before trying it.

## Where Kegels Can Help

Pelvic floor training can help men with after-dribble, according to [University Hospitals Sussex](https://www.uhsussex.nhs.uk/resources/male-pelvic-floor-exercises/). First, learn a controlled inward lift with normal breathing and a clear release afterward.

A continence nurse or physiotherapist can check the movement and suggest an appropriate routine. There is no reason to treat every toilet visit as an extra workout.

Our [guide to finding your pelvic floor muscles](/articles/how-to-find-pelvic-floor-muscles-men/) can help you understand the movement before practicing.

## The Mistake to Avoid: Training While Peeing

Repeatedly stopping and starting the urine stream is not a daily Kegel routine. It can interfere with normal emptying. Practice separately, and let the pelvic floor relax while you urinate.

If squeezing causes discomfort or you struggle to release, get advice before increasing repetitions. [Pelvic floor relaxation](/articles/reverse-kegels-for-men/) is a different skill from squeezing harder.

## When It Is More Than After-Dribble

Arrange an assessment if leakage comes with a weak stream, trouble getting started, or a repeated feeling that your bladder is not empty. Do not assume all leakage proves weak muscles.

[NIDDK explains](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/urinary-retention/symptoms-causes) that retention can also involve blockage, impaired bladder contraction, or tight pelvic floor muscles.

If you cannot urinate, or have severe lower abdominal pain, seek urgent medical care.

## Make Training Easier to Follow

If strengthening is appropriate for you, Kegel Morse Hero can guide squeeze-and-rest timing. It is a practice aid, not a test for the cause of leakage or a promise that symptoms will disappear.

## Waking Up to Pee at Night? Kegels May Not Be the Answer
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/waking-up-to-pee-at-night/
Last reviewed: 2026-09-28

Another bathroom trip. Another look at the ceiling while you try to fall asleep again. If this keeps happening, it is tempting to assume your pelvic floor needs more exercise.

Waking from sleep to urinate is called nocturia. Kegels may belong in some bladder-care plans, but night waking alone does not tell you which treatment you need.

## One Symptom, Several Possible Causes

Sometimes the body makes more urine during the night. Sometimes the bladder signals urgency at smaller volumes. Prostate-related emptying problems, certain medicines, and sleep disorders can also contribute.

The [Royal Devon NHS leaflet](https://www.royaldevon.nhs.uk/media/lyoe1qxv/nocturia-and-nocturnal-polyuria-rd-25-007-001.pdf), issued in February 2025, separates nocturia from increased nighttime urine production. That distinction matters: stronger pelvic muscles do not directly switch off urine production.

## When Pelvic Floor Training May Fit

For an overactive bladder, pelvic floor exercises may be used alongside bladder retraining to help manage urgency. [Gateshead Health](https://www.gatesheadhealth.nhs.uk/resources/bladder-retraining/) describes this approach.

That does not establish Kegels as a universal nocturia treatment. If the problem is excess nighttime urine, an obstruction, or disrupted breathing during sleep, the underlying cause needs attention.

Avoid inventing a nighttime schedule that forces you to hold urine through discomfort.

## Keep a Three-Day Record

Before an appointment, write down:

- When and how much you drink.
- When you urinate and, if practical, the amount.
- Any urgency or leakage.
- Bedtime, waking time, and nighttime bathroom visits.

[NIDDK recommends a two-to-three-day bladder diary](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/bladder-control-problems/diagnosis) when investigating bladder control symptoms. Adding sleep times gives your clinician useful context for night waking.

The record does not diagnose the cause. It makes the conversation more specific than “I go a lot.”

## Changes Worth Discussing

Avoid large drinks close to bedtime and consider reducing evening caffeine or alcohol. Keep normal daytime hydration; do not deliberately dehydrate yourself to avoid the toilet.

If you have a prescribed fluid limit, follow your clinician's instructions. Ask about medication timing rather than moving or stopping doses yourself.

## Don't Overlook Sleep

Loud snoring, witnessed breathing pauses, gasping, and marked daytime tiredness are reasons to ask about sleep apnoea. The [NHS symptom guide](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sleep-apnoea/) explains what to look for.

Night waking plus those symptoms deserves more than a stronger Kegel routine.

## When to Get Checked

Book an appointment if repeated night trips disrupt sleep, especially with new urinary symptoms. If you cannot pass urine or have severe lower abdominal pain, seek urgent care; these can be signs of [urinary retention](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/urinary-retention/symptoms-causes).

## Use a Training App for the Right Job

If pelvic floor strengthening is part of your plan, Kegel Morse Hero can help you follow squeeze-and-rest timing. It does not determine why you wake at night.

For help keeping an appropriate routine consistent, read [How to Remember to Do Kegels](/articles/how-to-remember-to-do-kegels-every-day/).

## How to Do Kegels Without Doing Them Wrong
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/how-to-do-kegels-without-doing-them-wrong/
Last reviewed: 2026-09-28

You squeeze something, count to three, and hope it is the right muscle. Sound familiar? The tricky part of Kegels is that a lot of effort can feel convincing even when you are mostly clenching your butt or bracing your stomach.

This guide walks men through a simple technique check. Start with one controlled repetition before worrying about a daily total.

## First, Check That Strengthening Fits

If you already have pelvic pain, difficulty emptying your bladder, or symptoms that get worse with squeezing, get assessed before starting a strengthening routine.

A pelvic floor can have trouble relaxing as well as contracting. [Cleveland Clinic's guide to hypertonic pelvic floor](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/22870-hypertonic-pelvic-floor) explains why some people need treatment focused on restoring relaxation and coordination.

## Step 1: Find the Lift

Lie on your back with your knees bent, or sit comfortably with your feet supported. Let your thighs and buttocks relax.

Imagine stopping yourself from passing gas. Gently close around the back passage and draw the muscles inward and upward. Avoid pushing down as though trying to empty your bowels.

In men, the base of the penis may move slightly toward the abdomen during a contraction. This is a possible cue, not a pass-or-fail test. [University Hospitals Sussex](https://www.uhsussex.nhs.uk/resources/male-pelvic-floor-exercises/) describes the movement.

If you are still unsure what you are feeling, see [How to Find Your Pelvic Floor Muscles](/articles/how-to-find-pelvic-floor-muscles-men/).

## Step 2: Do One Complete Repetition

1. Start in a comfortable position, with no deliberate squeeze.
2. Lift the pelvic floor inward.
3. Hold for about three seconds while breathing normally.
4. Let the contraction go completely.
5. Rest for about three seconds, or longer if you need time to release.

This brief hold-and-rest pattern follows [Mayo Clinic's beginner guidance](https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/mens-health/in-depth/kegel-exercises-for-men/art-20045074). If you cannot maintain the hold without straining, shorten it. The goal is a controlled repetition, not winning a countdown.

## Step 3: Check What the Rest of Your Body Is Doing

| What you notice | What to try |
| --- | --- |
| You stop breathing | Pause, return to easy breathing, and retry with less effort. |
| Your buttocks clench or thighs squeeze together | Reset your position and focus on the small internal lift. |
| You brace your belly hard | Reduce the effort; let your abdomen move naturally with breathing. |
| You push downward | Stop and return to the inward-lift cue. Get help if the direction remains unclear. |
| You cannot feel yourself release | Rest longer instead of immediately adding another squeeze. |

These checks can highlight obvious mistakes, but they cannot confirm your technique as reliably as a professional assessment.

## Step 4: Build the Routine After the Movement

Try a few comfortable repetitions first. Mayo Clinic describes gradually working toward 10 to 15 repetitions per set, with three sets a day. That is general guidance, not a target everyone must reach immediately.

Your clinician may recommend a different hold, rest, or frequency. [NIDDK advises an individual exercise plan](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/kegel-exercises) and cautions against overdoing it.

As control improves, practice sitting and standing too. Keep the same attention on breathing and release.

## Keep Toilet Time Separate

Do not make stopping and restarting your urine stream a regular exercise. It can interfere with bladder emptying. The imagined “hold in gas” cue lets you practice away from the toilet.

And do not keep a background squeeze going all day. Between repetitions and sessions, let the muscles rest.

## Still Unsure? Get Feedback

If you cannot identify a clear lift and release, a pelvic floor physiotherapist can check what you are doing. Biofeedback may help you understand the contraction and relaxation.

Stop exercises that cause pain or worsening symptoms. For further reading, see [Am I Doing Kegels Wrong?](/articles/am-i-doing-kegels-wrong/) and [Reverse Kegels for Men](/articles/reverse-kegels-for-men/).

## Let the App Handle Timing

Once you know the movement and strengthening suits your plan, Kegel Morse Hero can guide squeeze-and-rest timing with Morse code patterns. It provides cues; it does not measure your contraction or verify which muscles you use.

[Explore Kegel Morse Hero on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/kegel-morse-hero-pelvic-floor/id6761460873)

## Constipated Despite Fiber? Your Pelvic Floor May Be Working Backwards
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/constipation-pelvic-floor-dysfunction/
Last reviewed: 2026-10-09

You added fiber. You drink more water. You walk, wait, and still feel as though the exit will not open. Sometimes the missing piece is not what is in the stool. It is how the muscles around the rectum coordinate when you try to pass it.

This is called a defecatory disorder or pelvic floor dyssynergia. It is one possible cause of constipation-not a diagnosis you can make from symptoms alone.

## A Bowel Movement Needs an Exit, Not Another Squeeze

During a normal bowel movement, pressure from the abdomen helps move stool down while the pelvic floor and anal sphincter relax. The puborectalis muscle also loosens its sling around the rectum so the passage becomes straighter.

With dyssynergia, the outlet muscles may fail to relax or may contract instead. [North Tees NHS](https://www.nth.nhs.uk/resources/obstructive-defaecation-syndrome-ods-also-known-as-anismus/) explains this coordination problem.

That is why "stronger" is not always the answer. A muscle can generate force and still be badly coordinated for the task.

## Clues That Deserve a Proper Assessment

Possible clues include:

- Regularly straining even when stool is not especially hard.
- Feeling blocked at the outlet.
- Spending a long time on the toilet without feeling empty.
- Needing to change position or use a finger to help stool pass.
- Constipation that persists despite reasonable fiber, fluid, and activity changes.

A clinician may use an examination, anorectal manometry, a balloon-expulsion test, or imaging. [ACG](https://gi.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-gi/constipation) describes assessment of pelvic floor coordination.

## Why More Kegels Can Miss the Problem

Standard Kegels train a deliberate contraction. But emptying requires the outlet to relax at the right moment. Repeatedly adding hard squeezes to a coordination problem does not teach that release and may leave you feeling more guarded.

Avoid prolonged straining. If you have pelvic pain, urinary hesitancy, or difficulty releasing a contraction, get assessed before increasing Kegel volume.

Our guide to [Reverse Kegels for Men](/articles/reverse-kegels-for-men/) explains the difference between gentle release and forceful bearing down, but it is not a substitute for diagnosing chronic constipation.

## What Biofeedback Actually Retrains

Biofeedback uses sensors to show pressure or muscle activity. A trained clinician helps you coordinate abdominal pressure with relaxation of the outlet muscles.

[NIDDK](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/constipation/treatment) describes muscle retraining. The 2024 ASCRS guideline recommends biofeedback for symptomatic pelvic floor dyssynergia.

That recommendation applies after the problem has been identified. A consumer Kegel timer cannot measure rectal pressure, diagnose dyssynergia, or reproduce therapist-guided bowel retraining.

## Make the Toilet Setup Less Difficult

For a comfortable bowel movement, sit rather than hover. Support your feet on a small stool so your knees are slightly higher than your hips, lean forward, and keep breathing instead of clamping your breath.

Follow individualized advice about fiber, fluids, activity, and medicines. Do not change prescriptions or increase laxatives without guidance.

## Know the Red Flags

Seek prompt care for bleeding, constant abdominal pain, inability to pass gas, vomiting, fever, or unexplained weight loss. See the NIDDK source below for details.

## Use the App for the Job It Can Do

Kegel Morse Hero can time squeeze-and-rest practice when strengthening is part of your plan. It is not a constipation treatment and cannot tell whether your pelvic floor is relaxing during a bowel movement.

[Explore Kegel Morse Hero on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/kegel-morse-hero-pelvic-floor/id6761460873)

## Leaking After Prostate Surgery? The Kegel Timeline Nobody Explains
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/kegels-after-prostate-surgery/
Last reviewed: 2026-10-09

Temporary leakage is common after radical prostatectomy. The catheter comes out, you stand up, and urine escapes before you can react. Understanding the recovery stages helps make pelvic floor training more manageable.

Here is the timeline that matters, including the point when more exercise is not the only next step.

## Before Surgery: Learn the Movement, Not a Marathon

The useful pre-surgery goal is to identify a clean pelvic floor lift while breathing normally and relaxing fully afterward. Learning the movement before soreness, fatigue, and a catheter complicate the picture can make it easier to restart later.

The 2024 AUA guideline discusses preoperative training, often started several weeks before surgery. Evidence varies, and no single ideal start date or dosage is established.

Follow the plan from your surgical team. A preoperative session with a pelvic health physiotherapist can be especially useful if you cannot tell whether you are lifting, pushing down, or clenching your buttocks.

## While the Catheter Is In: Pause the Kegels

[Prostate Cancer UK](https://prostatecanceruk.org/prostate-information-and-support/living-with-prostate-cancer/pelvic-floor-muscle-exercises) advises pausing exercises while a catheter is in place.

Exact restart instructions vary. Some teams say to begin immediately after removal; others wait a few days based on healing and bladder emptying. Your discharge instructions take priority over a generic online schedule.

If a catheter stops draining, leakage suddenly increases around it, or you have fever or severe pain, contact your care team rather than trying to squeeze through the problem.

## After Removal: Training May Speed the Early Recovery

The first weeks are often the wettest. Leakage may be worse when you stand, cough, walk, or tire later in the day. That does not tell you your final level of continence.

A [2024 review of nine trials](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39104234/) found better continence recovery at one, three, and six months with exercise. At 12 months the difference was not statistically significant.

That distinction matters: training may help you recover control sooner, but it is not a guarantee that every man will be dry by a certain date.

## Technique Beats Panic Reps

A postoperative program should be progressive. Start with the number and hold time your clinician recommends, and keep the release at least as deliberate as the squeeze.

Watch for common compensation:

- Holding your breath.
- Bracing your abdomen as hard as possible.
- Clenching your buttocks or thighs.
- Pushing downward instead of lifting inward.
- Doing extra sets every time you notice a leak.

Muscles tire. If control gets worse during or after a session, that is a reason to review the dose rather than double it. Do not repeatedly stop your urine stream as a training drill.

For a step-by-step movement check, read [How to Do Kegels Without Doing Them Wrong](/articles/how-to-do-kegels-without-doing-them-wrong/).

## Use the Pelvic Floor Before the Pressure Hits

Many leaks happen with a sudden rise in abdominal pressure. Once your team has cleared you to train, practice a quick, gentle lift just before standing, coughing, sneezing, or lifting. This anticipatory contraction is often called "the Knack."

It should not become an all-day clench. Release again after the effort passes.

## When Kegels Are Not the Whole Plan

Persistent bothersome leakage deserves follow-up. The AUA guideline discusses surgery from six months when conservative care is not helping, and at one year when bothersome stress incontinence persists.

Assessment can distinguish stress leakage, urgency, and emptying problems. Options may include supervised training, bladder strategies, a male sling, or an artificial urinary sphincter.

## Let the App Handle Timing After You Are Cleared

Kegel Morse Hero can guide squeeze-and-rest timing once your surgical team says pelvic floor strengthening is appropriate. It cannot judge wound healing, check catheter problems, measure leakage, or personalize postoperative rehabilitation.

[Explore Kegel Morse Hero on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/kegel-morse-hero-pelvic-floor/id6761460873)

- [Prostate Cancer UK: Pelvic Floor Muscle Exercises](https://prostatecanceruk.org/prostate-information-and-support/living-with-prostate-cancer/pelvic-floor-muscle-exercises)

## Can Kegels Fix Erectile Dysfunction? The Evidence Is Complicated
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/kegels-erectile-dysfunction/
Last reviewed: 2026-10-09

Search for a natural erectile dysfunction fix and you will quickly meet a confident promise: do Kegels, strengthen the right muscles, and erections will return. The anatomy makes that claim sound plausible. The clinical evidence is less tidy.

Pelvic floor training may help some men, but "Kegels fix ED" is far stronger than current research allows.

## Why the Pelvic Floor Is Part of an Erection

The ischiocavernosus and bulbocavernosus muscles help support penile rigidity and contribute to ejaculation. Their function is one reason pelvic floor training has been studied for ED.

But an erection also depends on blood vessels, nerves, hormones, arousal, medication effects, and mental health. Pelvic muscle strength is only one part of the system.

## The Study Behind Many Big Claims

A [2004 trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1324914/) enrolled 55 men. Exercises plus biofeedback and lifestyle advice improved erectile function more than lifestyle advice alone at three months.

That is encouraging, but it was a small study and did not test a timer-only Kegel routine. The package included professional feedback and lifestyle changes, and not every participant improved.

## Newer Reviews Do Not Give One Clear Answer

A [systematic review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38596771/) reported benefits from physiotherapy programs. Programs combined different interventions, so the contribution and ideal dose of each remain unclear.

A [2024 meta-analysis](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38937909/) found benefit from aerobic exercise, but no significant improvement in its pelvic floor training subgroup. Seven trials were included overall.

So the honest conclusion is not "Kegels never work." It is that evidence is mixed, programs differ, and we cannot promise that a generic set of contractions will treat ED.

## Erectile Dysfunction Is a Symptom, Not One Disease

[NIDDK](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/erectile-dysfunction/symptoms-causes) describes vascular, hormonal, neurological, medication, and psychological causes of ED.

Recurring ED deserves a medical assessment. History, examination, blood pressure, and selected tests can help identify the cause.

Do not stop a prescribed medicine because you suspect it affects erections. Ask the prescriber to review it.

## When Pelvic Floor Training May Still Fit

A clinician may include pelvic floor training when muscles are weak or poorly coordinated. A plan can address contraction, endurance, quick responses, and full relaxation.

Get technique checked if you cannot isolate a lift. Pelvic pain or urinary hesitancy deserves assessment before strengthening. See [Can You Do Too Many Kegels?](/articles/can-you-do-too-many-kegels/).

## A Better First Plan Than Chasing a Miracle Routine

1. Get recurring ED evaluated, especially if it is new or worsening.
2. Review cardiovascular, metabolic, hormonal, medication, and psychological factors with a clinician.
3. Ask whether supervised pelvic floor training is appropriate for your specific cause.
4. Keep regular aerobic activity in the conversation; the 2024 review found stronger evidence for it than for pelvic floor training alone.
5. Treat Kegels as a possible adjunct, not a substitute for established ED care.

## Use Guided Timing Without the Promise

If pelvic floor strengthening is part of your plan, Kegel Morse Hero can make squeeze-and-rest timing easier to follow. It does not diagnose erectile dysfunction, measure muscle activation, or guarantee better erections.

[Explore Kegel Morse Hero on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/kegel-morse-hero-pelvic-floor/id6761460873)

## Sources

- [Dorey et al.: Pelvic Floor Exercises and Biofeedback for Erectile Dysfunction, randomized trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1324914/)
- [Physiotherapy Interventions for Male Sexual Dysfunction: systematic review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38596771/)
- [Chen et al.: Exercise Training for Erectile Dysfunction, systematic review and meta-analysis (2024)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38937909/)
- [NIDDK: Symptoms and Causes of Erectile Dysfunction](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/erectile-dysfunction/symptoms-causes)
- [NIDDK: Diagnosis of Erectile Dysfunction](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/erectile-dysfunction/diagnosis)

## Best Actually Usable Free Option: Kegel Trainer PFM Exercises

Choose it if you want:

- Reminders and simple streak tracking.

Skip it if seeing an optional subscription at all is a deal-breaker or if a clinician has prescribed a highly specific rehabilitation routine.

[Squeeze Time for Men](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/squeeze-time-for-men-kegel/id1395804535) is free to download. Its US listing shows one Premium in-app purchase at $4.99 rather than a recurring plan.

## Where Kegel Morse Hero Fits

[Kegel Morse Hero](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/kegel-morse-hero-pelvic-floor/id6761460873) is free to download and uses Morse-code rhythms, visual animation, and haptic feedback to guide short contractions and longer holds.

It is not accurate to call it a no-subscription app. The current US listing shows weekly, monthly, and annual plans. It also shows a $29.99 Lifetime Premium purchase, which avoids recurring billing after the one-time payment.

Choose it if the main problem is that ordinary countdown timers become boring. Do not choose it because you need diagnosis, biofeedback, or a clinician-configured post-surgical plan; it does not provide those things.

## What “No Subscription” Should Mean Before You Tap Buy

Check these four details in the store listing and the purchase screen:

1. **Is the download free, or is the useful part free?** A free install can still lead directly to a paywall.
2. **Is the payment one-time?** Look for words such as “Premium” or “Lifetime,” then confirm that the purchase is not described as auto-renewing.
3. **Is there a trial?** A trial may convert to a weekly, monthly, or annual plan unless cancelled.
4. **Can you restore the purchase?** A lifetime or one-time unlock should normally be restorable through the same store account.

The App Store purchase sheet shown immediately before confirmation is the final price to trust.

## Do You Need a Paid Kegel App at All?

You may not need one if you can already perform the correct contraction and follow a clinician-approved routine with a normal timer.

Paying can make sense when an app solves a specific adherence problem:

- You forget sessions without reminders.
- You lose count during holds and rests.
- Haptic cues let you train without watching the screen.
- Custom programming reproduces instructions from a physiotherapist.
- A more engaging format keeps you consistent.

An app cannot determine whether your pelvic floor is weak, overactive, painful, or poorly coordinated. Stop and get assessed if training causes pelvic pain, urinary hesitancy, worsening urgency, or difficulty relaxing.
